records.name: North Carolina
records.current_summary: The archetype of legislative instability: HB 2 (2016) restricted bathrooms to birth-certificate sex and was repealed in 2017 after mass backlash, but a binary-“sex” statute remains. Trans-murder monitoring data places North Carolina at about 3.0 killings per 100k trans women — a recorded floor, mid-pack among states with documented killings — and the July 2026 legal-risk map classifies it moderate-risk (alongside Alaska and Kentucky). Below the national score 0.36.

sources.claim: The Needle investigative essay (16 July 2026): a national data analysis comparing legal-risk tiers with Trans Murder Monitoring kill records, arguing protective statutes do not predict lower lethal risk for trans women; includes a state rate chart in which North Carolina stands at 3.0 killings per 100k trans women with 3+ recorded victims (an acknowledged undercount) and characterises North Carolina as moderate-risk.

sources.title: North Carolina's transgender bathroom battle: what sparked it, and what's next | North Carolina | The Guardian
sources.claim: Explainer of HB 2's origins: after the Charlotte city council in March 2016 passed an ordinance allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity, the state legislature in emergency session passed House Bill 2, which bars cities from passing anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people. The law drew global backlash with companies including Google and Disney pledging to pull back business, and the U.S. Justice Department called HB 2 'state-sponsored discrimination' and sued, with North Carolina filing its own suit. Names HB 2 as the archetype bathroom bill behind this record.

sources.title: A State Divided: HB2 And Transgender Rights | WUNC News
sources.claim: WUNC's North Carolina series on House Bill 2 states that the law requires people to use public bathrooms that correspond with the sex listed on their birth certificate, and records that on March 30, 2017 legislators in the North Carolina General Assembly passed a measure that repealed House Bill 2. Covers both the birth-certificate-sex bathroom rule and its 2017 repeal by the state legislature, matching this record's HB 2 arc.

sources.title: NC Republicans push new bathroom bill years after boycotts over similar legislation :: WRAL.com
sources.claim: WRAL, March 25, 2025: North Carolina made national news in 2016 for transgender bathroom rules that Republicans later repealed in the face of boycotts, and GOP lawmakers in the 2025 session are again pushing a bathroom bill. Shows the state's facility-use policy remains an active legislative subject years after HB 2, supporting the record's 'archetype of legislative instability' framing.

records.name: Missouri
records.current_summary: Bans gender-affirming medical care for minors (the SAFE Act, in force since 28 August 2023 after a judge declined to block it) and restricts access to such treatment for people in prisons, jails and correctional centres, with providers facing licence revocation; no adult facility ban recorded. Slightly below the national score 0.36.
records.current_localsOnly: The minors-care ban, the Medicaid (MO HealthNet) coverage exclusion and the 2027 sunset bind residents and their providers; a visitor's exposure is the institutional posture they signal, not these mechanisms.

sources.claim: PBS NewsHour report (29 August 2023, St Louis): a judge denied a preliminary injunction against Missouri's ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors, so the Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act took effect 28 August 2023 — prohibiting hormones/puberty blockers for under-18s (unless already in treatment) and all transition-related surgeries for minors; the law also bars MO HealthNet Medicaid coverage, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, exposes violating providers to licence revocation, and sunsets in 2027 after a Republican–Democrat concession; plaintiffs (ACLU of Missouri, Lambda Legal and others) continue toward trial on the merits.

sources.title: Missouri Ends Gender-Affirming Care for Transgender Inmates
sources.claim: Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe signed an appropriations law, effective July 2, 2026, that bars any state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Metro Weekly reports Missouri thereby became the seventh US state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban gender-affirming care for inmates; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while similar Idaho and Georgia measures were blocked by federal courts. This documents the record's claim that Missouri restricts such treatment for people in prisons and jails.

sources.title: Missouri ban on gender-affirming care for minors upheld by judge
sources.claim: A Missouri judge on November 25, 2024 upheld Senate Bill 49, the 2023 state law prohibiting gender-affirming care for minors; Lambda Legal and the ACLU of Missouri, counsel for the plaintiffs, said they would appeal. CNN reports the law also bars Missouri Medicaid from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, and that doctors who violate the ban can lose their Missouri medical licence and be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment. The ruling confirms the care ban the record describes as in force since August 28, 2023.

sources.title: Missouri Supreme Court upholds ban on minor transgender care
sources.claim: The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld the state's ban on gender-transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other gender-affirming care for minors on January 13, 2026, quoting the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's similar ban. STLPR notes the SAFE Act ban enacted in 2023 is set to expire in 2027, that lawmakers want to make it permanent, and that a November 2026 ballot initiative also seeks to ban such care indefinitely. The ruling shows the ban remains enforced and is moving toward permanence rather than being struck down.

sources.title: Families and Medical Providers Sue Missouri to Block Transgender Youth Medical Care Ban
sources.claim: Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner filed suit on July 25, 2023, in Cole County Circuit Court to block implementation of Missouri's Senate Bill 49, which prevents transgender adolescents from accessing gender-affirming medical care and was scheduled to take effect August 28, 2023. Plaintiffs were three families of transgender young people, medical providers, and PFLAG National and GLMA. The filing documents the effective date of the care ban the record says is in force.

records.name: Alaska
records.current_summary: Moderate tier in the July 2026 legal-risk assessment (grouped with Kentucky and North Carolina): one or two laws aimed at transgender adults or several aimed at youth, but no adult facility ban recorded and no protective statute. Slightly below the national score 0.36.

sources.claim: Erin In The Morning's anti-trans national legal-risk assessment map, July 2026 update (reposted by Stonewall News): Alaska appears in the Moderate-Risk group (AK, KY, NC) — states that "have either passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults or have enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly" — above the worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below the protective/safe groupings.

sources.title: Alaska medical board set to vote on restricting treatment of transgender minors
sources.claim: Alaska's State Medical Board, whose members are appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy, was set to vote at its August 22, 2025 meeting on formally opposing 'treatment of gender dysphoria in minors' and on a statement opposing late-term abortion, after a board member proposed the resolution in June 2025. The Anchorage Daily News reports Dunleavy's earlier bid to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, but a board he appointed limited transgender girls' participation in girls' sports teams. The item documents Alaska's regulatory rather than legislative pressure on transgender care, consistent with the record's moderate-tier 'laws aimed at youth' profile.

sources.title: Mat-Su transgender bathroom ban becomes permanent in apparent first for Alaska
sources.claim: The Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District board in Alaska voted 5-1 on October 19, 2022 to permanently adopt a policy requiring transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex at birth or a private option such as the nurse's office, overturning guidelines in place for more than seven years. AP reports the policy was described as an apparent first for Alaska. As a school-district policy it is not a state adult facility ban, matching the record's finding that no adult facility ban is recorded for Alaska.

sources.title: Alaska medical board seeks to restrict abortion, transgender medical care
sources.claim: Alaska's health-care regulatory board voted unanimously on August 22, 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation that would classify providing gender-transition care to anyone under 18 as 'unprofessional conduct', subject to disciplinary action. The Alaska Beacon story reports the draft regulation must be vetted by the Alaska Department of Law and then undergo a 30-day public comment period. No adult-facility or adult-care ban is involved, consistent with the record's moderate grading for Alaska.

records.name: Georgia
records.current_summary:
A July 2026 data analysis places Georgia's recorded killing rate for trans women at 4.8 per 100k per year — among the country's highest — and a Georgia law-review article documents the long-run fatality concentration around Atlanta: at least 15 fatal cases statewide across 1990–2014 (11 in Atlanta) and 16 more across 2015–2023 (8 in Atlanta). Both series are treated by their authors as undercount floors.

The same analysis's warning applies to Georgia directly: its legal-risk grade describes how the state behaves, not how its people do — here a jurisdiction whose documented danger to trans people has been violence on the street more than legislation from the legislature.

sources.claim: The Needle (July 2026) state-by-state analysis overlaying legislative-risk maps on recorded trans-homicide data: legal risk predicts how the state treats you, not how people do; this state's recorded killing rate for trans women is 4.8 per 100k/yr — all counts acknowledged floors from an undercounted monitoring project.

sources.title: Georgia's governor signs ban on certain gender-affirming care for minors
sources.claim: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp on March 23, 2023 signed Senate Bill 140, barring licensed medical professionals from providing patients under 18 with hormone therapy or surgery related to gender transition, with licence revocation as a possible penalty; minors who began hormone replacement therapy before July 1, 2023 may continue under the law. CNN reports the ACLU of Georgia said it would sue. The ban took effect July 1, 2023, giving an on-the-ground legal restriction relevant to a trans traveller's assessment of Georgia.

sources.title: Georgia agrees to pay for gender-affirming care for public employees
sources.claim: In October 2023 plaintiffs announced a settlement with Georgia's State Health Benefit Plan in Atlanta federal court, requiring the plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, spouses and dependents, after a December 2022 lawsuit argued the plan illegally discriminated by refusing to pay. The story notes the plan could then be required to pay for care for minors outside Georgia even though prohibited inside the state. This documents that Georgia's public-employee health plan coverage for gender-affirming care continued by settlement despite the 2023 care ban.

sources.title: Atlanta police investigating 3 'violent crimes' against transgender women
sources.claim: Atlanta police said in April 2023 they were actively investigating three 'violent crimes' against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart; a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open. ABC News quotes the Atlanta Police Department acknowledging the 'epidemic-level violence black and brown transgender women face in America'. The story supports the record's finding that Georgia's documented danger to trans people has been street violence concentrated in Atlanta.

sources.title: Memorial Health halts transgender surgeries: 5 things to know
sources.claim: Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah abruptly cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries on February 13, 2025, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man, citing a responsibility to follow state and federal laws and regulations that appears to reference the January 28, 2025 federal executive order denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. The Current reports Savannah Pride Center said at least two other area residents were also denied care. This documents on-the-ground shrinkage of adult gender-affirming care access in Georgia under federal funding pressure.

records.name: Virginia
records.current_summary:
A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Virginia among its 'low-risk states' group — largely refraining from targeting transgender adults — while noting Virginia has enacted anti-trans policies affecting trans youth that the map's author considers unlikely to be extended to adults.

The state's school-focused facility restriction (2023) is recorded in a national equality tracker, though the tracker's cited page has since moved; the practical exposure for a visitor in Virginia therefore sits with the youth-policy record rather than any statute aimed at adult public life.
records.current_localsOnly: Virginia's 2023 K-12 facility ban reaches school facilities — school-aged users are residents; a visitor's exposure to it is limited.

sources.claim: July 2026 assessment: Virginia in its Low-Risk States group (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC); explicitly named with Arizona as a state that enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies that, due to state-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

records.name: District of Columbia
records.current_summary: Downgraded from “most protective”: as a federal district, Congress and the executive reach it directly — Congress attached a bathroom ban for DC, and activists protesting it at the Capitol were arrested (Dec 2024). Its protective local-law layer persists but is overridable; direction: mixed, downgraded from its former most-protective placement.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (Axios returned 403 to automated fetch); the underlying Axios report (5 Dec 2024) covers transgender-rights activists arrested while protesting at the Capitol against the bathroom ban Congress attached to the District of Columbia.

July 2026 assessment: DC may no longer be considered 'most protective' because it can fall under attack from Congress and executive actions; DC appears in the assessment's Low-Risk States list (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC).

freshness_all.fact: Cited Dec 2024 Capitol bathroom-protest arrests are historical record (do not stale); DC itself has no ban and protective code unchanged.

records.name: Maine
records.current_summary: Assessed comparatively protected (low-risk tier, July 2026) — but rose in risk after the University of Maine system capitulated to federal pressure on trans sports participation rather than defending its trans students and athletes: the system affirmed compliance with the new federal rules once the Department of Agriculture suspended its federal funding (March 2025). Direction: better than the country overall, with an upward risk signal.

sources.claim: July 2026 assessment: Maine in its Low-Risk States group, with the assessment separately flagging that Maine has increased in risk due to capitulation over sports bans in the University of Maine system.

NBC News (21 Mar 2025, upd. 24 Mar): University of Maine System announced compliance with federal restrictions on trans sports participation after the US Department of Agriculture suspended federal funding for research and programs while investigating possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes.

records.name: Delaware
records.current_summary:
A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Delaware in its 'low-risk states' group — states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection; nothing in Delaware's record rises above that description in either direction.

A national equality tracker records no public-facility-use ban for Delaware. A September 2026 status check likewise found no enacted facility ban, while flagging that the tracker's own citation (a page since relocated) still awaits one manual re-verification.

sources.claim: July 2026 assessment lists Delaware in its Low-Risk States group (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC): states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (HTTP 404 at the archived URL); the underlying Movement Advancement Project equality map tracks state-by-state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity and records no such ban for Delaware.
